assumptions: Metric: assumed p95_latency_ms was the closest governed metric, but the result shown is the average (mean) latency of failed attempts computed via custom SQL.
Time: assumed the explicit window 2024-10-31..2026-10-31 for the past two years.
Period: the data actually available covers 2026-08-01..2026-10-31.
caveats: Data starts on 2026-08-01; the requested two-year window was clipped, so this is not a true two-year average.

Part of this answer uses custom SQL written by the AI, outside the governed semantic layer. It was validated (read-only, governed views only, role filters applied) before running, but its logic has not been reviewed like the governed metrics.

Duplicate records on 12 Oct: 341 attempts were ingested twice (11,704 raw rows vs 11,363 unique attempts, +3.0%). Paysight counts each attempt once; duplicates were removed in the clean view (first ingestion kept).

Missing issuer IDs: 8.0% of Meridian Bank's card attempts in 2026-08 (2,856 of 35,507) have no issuer_id; expected 0%. Issuer-level results for this scope are understated. Not corrected: rows are kept and shown as '(missing)' issuer.

Volume spike 18 Oct–31 Oct: attempt volume was +39% versus the usual level for those weekdays over 14 days. This may be a sale or a data gap; check before comparing totals across this period. Not a data error by itself.

facts.text: Technical failures averaged 17,422 ms authorization latency across 23,887 failed attempts.
Customer drop-off failures averaged 12,018 ms authorization latency across 45,910 failed attempts.
Risk declines averaged 3,204 ms authorization latency across 12,544 failed attempts.
Issuer declines averaged 2,559 ms authorization latency across 37,617 failed attempts.
The query covered a 400-day window (2025-10-02 to 2026-10-31) because the validator rejected the full two-year span; the underlying data only begins on 2026-08-01.
Data-quality scan found 341 duplicated attempts on 12 Oct (11,704 raw rows vs 11,363 unique), which were removed in the clean view the analysis used.

response.headline: Failed payments take very different times to authorize depending on why they failed: technical failures average about 17.4 seconds and customer drop-offs about 12.0 seconds, while issuer declines (2.6 seconds) and risk declines (3.2 seconds) are much faster. A single overall average and a full two-year view are not available, because the data only starts on 2026-08-01.

hypotheses.how_to_verify: Look at the latency distribution (median, p95, and share of attempts hitting the timeout threshold) within each failure category and compare against configured timeout values.
hypotheses.rationale: The long averages for technical and drop-off categories are consistent with waiting on timeouts, while declines return quickly; the evidence shows the pattern but not the mechanism.
hypotheses.text: Technical failures and customer drop-offs are slow mainly because they involve timeouts or abandoned sessions, whereas issuer and risk declines are fast explicit responses.

recommendations.linked_fact_or_hypothesis: Technical failures averaged 17,422 ms vs issuer declines at 2,559 ms.
recommendations.rationale: Averages differ by roughly 7x between categories, so a single number would hide where the slowness sits.
recommendations.text: Report latency for failed payments by failure category rather than as one blended average.

recommendations.linked_fact_or_hypothesis: Technical failures and customer drop-offs are slow mainly because of timeouts or abandoned sessions.
recommendations.rationale: These two categories have the highest latency and the largest combined share of failed attempts' wait time.
recommendations.text: Investigate the timeout behaviour behind technical failures and customer drop-offs.

recommendations.linked_fact_or_hypothesis: The query covered a 400-day window but data only begins on 2026-08-01.
recommendations.rationale: The catalog only exposes p95 latency, so this result relied on unreviewed custom SQL, and the data covers about three months rather than two years.
recommendations.text: Get the governed semantic layer extended with an average-latency metric and revisit this question once more history is loaded.
